subject: ba
title: Globalisation and Global Warming
objectives: Define globalisation and identify its main drivers.
Analyse the benefits and challenges of globalisation for businesses and economies.
Understand the link between globalisation and global warming.
Evaluate policy responses and business implications of climate change.
study:
Globalisation is the speed-up of movements and exchanges — of people, goods, services, capital, technology and culture — across the planet. The World Health Organization frames it as two interrelated elements: international borders opening to faster flows of goods, services, finance, people and ideas, plus the institutional and policy changes that enable those flows. It has two components: Globalisation of Markets (historically distinct national markets merging into one global marketplace) and Globalisation of Production (firms sourcing inputs from wherever cost and quality are best).

Key termContainerisation — standardised shipping containers that sharply cut sea-freight costs, making international goods movement cheaper and global markets genuinely contestable. One of the most underrated drivers of globalisation.

Other drivers include trade liberalisation, capital market integration, labour mobility, the rise of institutions like the IMF and World Bank, and reduced protectionism generally. Benefits include specialisation and productive efficiency, freer capital flow to wherever returns are highest, technology transfer, improved living standards, and a useful side-effect: bad domestic economic policy now risks real international isolation, which disciplines governments somewhat.

Exam tipGlobalisation's challenges are frequently tested with real Nigerian examples — capital flight from loss of financial-system confidence is the chapter's specific illustration, not a generic point.

Challenges include over-dependence on other countries, capital flight risk, loss of local culture as practices converge, environmental degradation from importing polluting goods, and local businesses collapsing under competition from larger foreign firms. Policy responses include good governance, economic liberalisation, strengthening multilateral institutions (IMF, World Bank, WTO), and investing in human capital and R&D.

Global warming, per NASA, is the long-term heating of Earth's surface due to human activity — primarily fossil fuel burning — raising greenhouse gas levels. It's the cause of climate change, not the same thing. 2011–2020 was the warmest decade on record, with 2019 reaching 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels; the international community (via the Paris Agreement) aims to keep warming well below 2°C, pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C specifically. Effects include more frequent droughts, storms and heat waves, rising sea levels, and damage to marine ecosystems and human livelihoods.

For business, global warming cuts both ways: it's a risk (regulatory compliance costs, supply chain disruption, reputational exposure) and an opportunity (green technology innovation, sustainable product development, access to ESG-linked investment) — increasingly a factor in corporate strategy rather than a side issue.
recap:
• Globalisation = accelerating global exchange of people/goods/capital/culture; components = Globalisation of Markets + Globalisation of Production.
  • Key drivers: technology, trade liberalisation, capital mobility, containerisation (cheaper shipping).
  • Benefits: specialisation/efficiency, capital flow, tech transfer, discourages bad domestic policy.
  • Challenges: dependence, capital flight risk, loss of culture, environmental degradation, local business collapse.
  • Policy responses: good governance, liberalisation, multilateral institutions (IMF/World Bank/WTO), human capital investment.
  • Global warming (NASA def) = long-term heating from human activity/GHGs; causes climate change. 2011–2020 warmest decade on record (+1.1°C by 2019); Paris Agreement targets 1.5°C.
  • Business implications: risk (compliance costs, disruption) vs opportunity (green tech, ESG investment).

quiz.q: Globalisation is best described as:
opts: A term with no relevance to modern business
The speed-up of movements and exchanges of people, goods, services, capital and culture all over the planet
A synonym for complete economic isolation
A process limited exclusively to a single country's internal trade

quiz.q: According to the World Health Organization, globalisation comprises two interrelated elements: the opening of international borders to fast flows of goods/services/finance/people/ideas, and:
opts: The complete elimination of all national governments
Changes in institutions and policies that facilitate or promote such flows
The abolition of all currencies worldwide
A total ban on any international travel

quiz.q: The Globalisation of Markets refers to:
opts: The complete separation of all national markets from each other
A synonym for protectionism
The merging of historically distinct national markets into one huge global marketplace
Only the domestic market of a single country

quiz.q: The Globalisation of Production refers to firms:
opts: Eliminating the need for any supply chain management
Refusing to trade with any foreign supplier
Producing goods only within their home country with no international sourcing
Sourcing goods and services from different parts of the world to exploit national differences in cost/quality of production factors

quiz.q: Which of the following is a factor responsible for globalisation, according to the chapter?
opts: Total prohibition of capital movement across borders
Universal rejection of new technology
Complete elimination of international trade
Trade liberalisation and technological change

quiz.q: Containerisation contributed to globalisation primarily by:
opts: Having no impact whatsoever on international trade
Eliminating all sea transport entirely
Increasing the cost of shipping goods internationally
Reducing the cost of sea shipping, making international goods movement cheaper and markets more contestable

quiz.q: Which of the following is a benefit of globalisation identified in the chapter?
opts: Guaranteed loss of foreign exchange earnings
Total collapse of all local businesses with no exception
Promotion of trade, specialisation and increased productive efficiency
Complete elimination of international communication

quiz.q: According to the chapter, globalisation can help reduce government excesses in fiscal and monetary policy because:
opts: Bad government policy risks international isolation in an interconnected world
The world operates in complete economic isolation
Fiscal policy has no international dimension at all
Governments have no international obligations whatsoever

quiz.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage/challenge of globalisation identified in the chapter?
opts: Loss of culture as traditions and customs change due to integration
Guaranteed elimination of all economic interdependence
Complete absence of any capital flow risk
Total immunity from foreign economic influence

quiz.q: The example of a country's economy experiencing massive capital outflow is cited in the chapter to illustrate:
opts: A purely historical event with no ongoing relevance
A disadvantage of globalisation relating to loss of confidence in a country's financial system
A benefit of globalisation with no downside
An example unrelated to globalisation

quiz.q: One recommended policy response to the challenges of globalisation is:
opts: Strengthening multilateral institutions such as the IMF, World Bank and WTO
Banning all forms of trade liberalisation
Complete withdrawal from all international engagement
Eliminating human capital development entirely

quiz.q: According to Ayodele and Stephen (2009), the 'Industrial' (Transnationalisation) aspect of globalisation refers to:
opts: Only the political governance of a single nation
Only domestic labour laws
Only the price of a single commodity
The emergence of worldwide production markets and broader access to foreign products

quiz.q: The 'Ecological' aspect of globalisation, per Ayodele and Stephen (2009), relates to:
opts: Global environmental challenges requiring international cooperation, such as climate change and pollution
Only the price of domestic real estate
Only a single country's internal agricultural policy
Only a nation's currency exchange rate

quiz.q: Effectively managing globalisation in a business, according to the chapter, requires:
opts: Complete avoidance of any research into target markets
Ignoring all local laws and regulations entirely
Thorough market research, effective cross-border communication, and compliance with local laws
Refusing to communicate with international stakeholders

quiz.q: According to NASA's definition cited in the chapter, Global Warming is:
opts: A phenomenon with no connection to human activity
The long-term heating of Earth's surface due to human activities, primarily fossil fuel burning, increasing greenhouse gas levels
A term identical in every respect to 'weather' with no distinction
A short-term, single-day temperature fluctuation

quiz.q: According to the chapter, global warming is the cause of:
opts: Currency devaluation
Trade liberalisation
Climate change
Capital market integration

quiz.q: The decade 2011-2020 is cited in the chapter as:
opts: Irrelevant to global warming discussions
The warmest decade on record, with global average temperature 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels by 2019
The coldest decade ever recorded
A decade with no measurable temperature change

quiz.q: The international community has recognised the need to keep global warming well below 2°C, pursuing efforts to limit it to:
opts: 0°C with no increase whatsoever

quiz.q: Which of the following is an effect of global warming/climate change identified in the chapter?
opts: No impact whatsoever on marine ecosystems
A guaranteed decrease in sea levels worldwide
More frequent and intense droughts, storms and heat waves
Complete elimination of all weather patterns

quiz.q: Global warming presents businesses with both risk and opportunity; opportunities mentioned in the chapter include:
opts: Green technology innovation, sustainable product development, and access to ESG-linked investment
Complete elimination of the need for any corporate strategy
Guaranteed avoidance of all regulatory compliance costs
Total immunity from reputational risk
